rationale: The judgment changed, so a complete new assessment is returned. Three things drove it. (1) The incumbent assessment had no steelman and no visible two-axis grading; both are required. (2) Two per-claim verdicts did not match the ledger the incumbent's own synthesis described: GEO-C020 was graded weakly_supported while three strong undermining records (E018, E019, E020) and one moderate (E021) face two moderate supporting records (E012, E017) with genuine physical-object disputes on both sides — that is a collision, so it is now 'mixed', with the synthesis stating plainly that the balance leans against for the tested recipe; GEO-C004 was graded 'mixed' although nothing in the ledger undermines it — as worded it is a descriptive claim about what two peer-reviewed papers report, so credibility is now 'provisionally_supported' while its diagnosticity is graded low, which is the two-axis separation the method demands. (3) The ledger gained GEO-E026 (the proponents' own statement of the salt observation) and research items GEO-R009–R011; GEO-C506 is therefore featured with a treatment, and the crux order is extended with the paleomagnetic survey (R011) leading as the only proposed test of the Great Pyramid claim independent of contested sample provenance, followed by the Iwawe desk check (R009), which moves the Andean claim for the price of reading. GEO-C903 is not featured: its only evidence record was declined and the featured set should not exceed what the ledger's records earn (fifteen claims). The article is retold from the ledger: the Egyptian exchange is laid out symmetrically with the recipe shift made explicit; the salt story is told with its wrong comparator; the phrase 'nobody has looked' is dropped (the report's blocked sources show the primary Arabic record has been examined even though it cannot yet be cited); unledgered biographical details (nationalities, 'funded laboratory research', a 1979 date) are removed; plate IMG-GEO-P05 (Rekhmire) is seated for the first time and the four incumbent plates are retained; and 'what would change our mind' is made an explicit section with both directions.
article:
At the granite quarries of Aswan, beside the largest abandoned obelisk in Egypt, there is a block that visitors are invited to hit. The idea is charming: pick up one of the rounded dolerite balls that ancient quarrymen are said to have used, strike the granite, and feel the past in your hands. Guides have been running this accidental experiment for decades. According to the proponent literature, [no visitor has ever managed to reproduce one of the smooth, scooped depressions that cover the quarry walls]{claim=GEO-C002}. The stones bounce. The granite shrugs.

{plate:IMG-GEO-P01}

An anecdote like this proves nothing by itself. Nobody has counted the attempts, and nobody has surveyed the test block for wear. But it points at the right question, which is not *who* built the monuments — nobody serious disputes that Egyptians built the pyramids or that the people of the Titicaca basin built Tiwanaku — but *how* the hardest stone was worked. The megalithic casting hypothesis gives a heterodox answer: some of it was never worked at all. It was made — mixed, moulded and set in place, the way concrete is made — from crushed rock, mineral binders and chemistry that a Bronze Age society could plausibly command.

{plate:IMG-GEO-P02}

The idea has a serious pedigree and a disreputable neighbourhood. The chemist Joseph Davidovits and his Geopolymer Institute have argued it since the late 1970s; a small body of peer-reviewed work supports it and a somewhat larger body rejects it. The hypothesis also circulates in a media ecosystem of lost civilisations and ancient machines with which this case has nothing to do. Casting needs no aliens and no forgotten engines — only forgotten chemistry, and chemistry is a documented kind of thing to forget. That is what makes it testable. What follows is what the testing has actually shown, where it has been done, and where it has not.

## The conventional account, taken seriously

Any honest map of this dispute starts by giving the orthodoxy its due, because the orthodoxy is strong.

The carved-and-transported account is not a guess. Quarries exist with unfinished monuments still attached to bedrock — the Aswan obelisk itself is the famous example, abandoned after the granite cracked. Stone tools have been recovered in quantity. Worker settlements survive at Giza. Experimental archaeologists have carved granite with dolerite and copper, slowly but genuinely. And modern geochemistry has matched monument stone to specific quarries. At Stonehenge, an immobile-trace-element study found that fifty of the fifty-two sarsens share one geochemical profile, and that Stone 58's signature directly matches the West Woods area about twenty-five kilometres away.

The conventional account's gaps are quantitative, not existential. Nowhere does it need a miracle. What it needs, in a few specific places, is more time, more labour or better technique than anyone has yet demonstrated. Those places are where this case lives.

## Egypt: the one monument where the stone has been tested

The Great Pyramid is the only disputed monument whose stone has been examined for a binder by parties on both sides. The exchange is worth walking through slowly, because its shape — not its headline — is what the case turns on.

The affirmative case rests on two laboratory papers. In 2006 a materials-science group at Drexel University led by M. W. Barsoum compares pyramid limestone samples under scanning and transmission electron microscopes with six natural limestones from the vicinity. It reports silicon-bearing microconstituents combined with calcium and magnesium "in ratios that do not exist in any of the potential limestone sources", hydrated phases with calcite-like chemistries "not known to hydrate in nature", and amorphous silica consistent with rapid precipitation from an alkaline solution. The authors claim this for some samples only, and concede that nature "could have — however unlikely — produced all the microstructures examined herein." Five years later a partly overlapping team publishes solid-state NMR spectra of a casing stone from the Bent Pyramid at Dahshur and reads them as Tura limestone grains "cemented with an amorphous calcium-silicate gel formed by human intervention" — a lime-and-silica cement of the kind that lime and diatomaceous earth are known to form at room temperature. The wording is "suggest"; the study is one stone against two quarry comparators.

Notice what has happened to the recipe. Davidovits' original proposal was an alkali-activated aluminosilicate — a geopolymer in the strict sense. The 2011 binder is something else: a calcium-silicate gel, the chemistry of lime mortar rather than of geopolymers. Evidence against one is not automatically evidence against the other, and the ledger keeps them apart.

{plate:IMG-GEO-P03}

The negative case is broader and older. Field and laboratory petrography by R. L. Folk and D. H. Campbell, published in 1991 and 1992, finds in pyramid and temple blocks the things sedimentary rock has and concrete does not: bedding, burrows, sharp cross-sections of clams and fragile worm tubes, ripple lamination, and calcite-filled tectonic fractures that stop at the edges of individual blocks — cracks that formed in the ground and were then cut through. They observe quarrymen's tool marks and detect no zeolitic binder by any of several methods. In 1993 Harrell and Penrod examine the "Lauer sample" — an interior specimen the proponents themselves hold up as limestone aggregate in synthetic cement — and conclude it is natural Mokattam Formation limestone with "no evidence of the special textures and zeolite cement that must exist if the sample is concrete." In 2007 two further studies appear. The concrete petrographer D. Jana examines Great Pyramid casing stones side by side with natural Tura limestone and with a genuine geopolymeric limestone made by Davidovits' own group — a *positive control*, meaning a known example of the thing being searched for, included so that the method can be shown to detect it. The control's binder is plainly enriched in sodium, potassium and aluminium; no casing stone shows anything like it. The silicon-rich spheres that the Drexel study highlighted turn out to be opal-CT lepispheres, which occur in the natural Tura stone too. And Freestone and Middleton, working independently of all the other groups, examine a British Museum casing fragment with light microscopy, electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction and infrared spectroscopy and find "a natural limestone. There are no features which support the artificial, geopolymeric origin advocated by Davidovits and co-workers" — no air bubbles, no fibres, no crushed-and-reaggregated texture.

Two things keep this from being decisive, and neither is a matter of interpretation. The first is a fight over physical objects. Davidovits contends that the piece Harrell and Jana analysed was not the authentic Lauer sample — wrong thickness, missing a calcium-phosphate coating — while Jana reports finding and mapping exactly that coating on the piece he received. Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities, for its part, has stated that no permission was granted to take the Drexel samples and that their origin is unknown. The second is the recipe shift. Jana's positive control demonstrates that an *alkali* binder would be visible if present; it does not test for a calcium-silicate gel, and no published rebuttal of the 2011 NMR paper exists. A 2008 feature in *Chemical & Engineering News* also fixed the honest scope of the claim: Barsoum argued only that the tops, backing blocks and casings were cast, with the cores most likely cut stone.

So the claim [that some blocks of the Great Pyramid are cast reconstituted limestone]{claim=GEO-C020} sits, on the present record, as a genuine collision: peer-reviewed microscopy on one side, peer-reviewed petrography on the other, each side able to point at a sample dispute or an untested recipe on the other's. Our reading is that the balance leans against — every binder-aware examination of pyramid stone by a group outside the pro-casting circle has concluded natural rock — but "leans against" is not "settled," and the one test that would settle it has not been run. What the exchange does establish beyond argument is narrower: [convincing artificial limestone can be made at all from materials available to ancient builders]{claim=GEO-C012}. The Geopolymer Institute reports multi-ton demonstration blocks, and the lime-silica chemistry is textbook. Feasibility is the one rung of the ladder in good repair. It is also the rung that proves the least.

## The salt

Woven through the Egyptian argument is a story about salt. The Geopolymer Institute's account of the hypothesis recounts that when the caliph al-Ma'mun's men broke into the Great Pyramid around 820 AD [they found the interior chamber walls coated with a layer of salt]{claim=GEO-C003} — an odd thing, the argument runs, for a sealed structure of dry quarried limestone to do, and an expected thing for stone that set wet with natron in it. The same page reports that Davidovits, on visits between 1984 and 2003, picked up fragments of pyramid stone and "tasted these stones with his tongue: they were salty," whereas a piece of geological limestone was not. From this the proponents infer that [Great Pyramid stones carry surface salt that comparable natural limestone monuments do not]{claim=GEO-C506}.

Both halves of the story are weaker than they sound. The medieval report has not been traced, within this case, to any primary Arabic source; it stands as a secondary account on a proponent website. The taste test is uncontrolled — no quantities, no instrument, no named comparator specimen. And the comparator the proponents offer is the wrong one. They argue that if the salt were natural "all our cathedrals built with limestone should be covered with salt." But a cathedral in northern Europe is not the relevant control for a monument standing on the Mokattam limestone of the Giza plateau; the relevant control is unworked Giza bedrock and quarry faces, and no one has published that comparison. Salt also has mundane candidates — efflorescence from mortar, groundwater wicking, centuries of visitors in enclosed chambers. The salt story is therefore filed as an unresolved anchor rather than an anomaly: two modest tasks, tracing the medieval report and sampling the natural bedrock, would either make it real or dissolve it.

## The ingredients, and a mural

The version of the hypothesis developed by the independent researcher Marcell Fóti runs on natron — the naturally occurring alkaline salt that Egyptian glassmakers used as a flux. Here the mainstream literature is squarely on the proponents' side about availability: Egypt possessed [industrial-scale natron deposits at Wadi el Natrun and al-Barnuj, exploited from antiquity, with supply declining and giving way to plant ash in the seventh to ninth centuries AD]{claim=GEO-C011}. That is a peer-reviewed finding about glass and faience, and it establishes exactly what it says — the ingredient was there — and nothing about stone. Natron heated with silica yields sodium silicate, or waterglass, a genuine mineral binder, and [the roughly 850 °C this requires is within reach of charcoal and bellows]{claim=GEO-C010}; the case's only record for that is a proponent citation of early glassmaking, though the temperature itself is modest by the standards of ancient metallurgy. Fóti also proposes a discovery pathway — that [a fire pit used for years can accidentally cement its own ash into stone]{claim=GEO-C013} — which rests on a single unattributed anecdote and has never been replicated.

{plate:IMG-GEO-P05}

The hypothesis has one candidate picture of itself. An Eighteenth-Dynasty mural in the tomb of the vizier Rekhmire, conventionally read as bronze-founders casting a great door, shows rows of crucibles tended by men with poles over a large casting floor. Fóti argues that [the scale of the operation and the apparatus depicted fit mineral processing better than bronze work]{claim=GEO-C005}. Egyptology has not engaged the reinterpretation, and the scene's own inscriptions have not yet been brought to bear on it in this case. It is a proponent reading of a picture, and is graded as such.

## The Andes: peer-reviewed, one team, never rerun

{plate:IMG-GEO-P04}

The other laboratory evidence from a disputed monument comes from Pumapunku, the andesite-and-sandstone temple complex at Tiwanaku in Bolivia, whose H-shaped blocks with identical stepped recesses are among the most photographed stones in the argument. Two 2019 papers by Davidovits and colleagues, in *Materials Letters* and *Ceramics International*, [report SEM and petrographic features in the andesite, including organic matter, that the authors argue natural volcanic stone should not contain]{claim=GEO-C004}, and interpret them as the residue of an organo-mineral binder.

Those papers passed peer review. They also come from the hypothesis's principal proponents, from a single sample set whose chain of custody has been questioned, and no independent laboratory has re-examined the stone. Volcanic rocks can host organic and glassy phases naturally, and the criteria used to call these features artificial have never been tested blind against andesite of known natural origin. The only counterweight in the record is a 1971 Bolivian Academy of Sciences study attributing Pumapunku's *red sandstones* to natural quarries — a different lithology, analysed with pre-modern methods. The two lines of evidence do not so much conflict as pass each other in the dark. That is why [the claim that Pumapunku's andesite and sandstone were geopolymer-cast]{claim=GEO-C021} is graded mixed: the sandstone half faces a provenance attribution, the andesite half has a proponent-only positive, and neither half has been tested by anyone else.

A cheap desk test exists. The proponents' own 2020 model specifies where the andesite aggregate came from — natural volcanic sand from Cerro Khapia, stored at the lakeshore site of Iwawe — and holds that the roughly dressed blocks found abandoned in transit were not building material. Reading the Iwawe excavators' own description of that deposit, and what independent fieldwork documents about carved andesite blocks en route from the mountain, would move this claim in one direction or the other without a single new sample from the monument.

## Aswan: the rate

Return to the quarry where we began. For a century the standard account of granite extraction rested largely on R. Engelbach's 1922 report on the unfinished obelisk. Per the proponents' reading — which the case has not yet checked against the monograph itself — its experimental basis was a single self-conducted hour of pounding with no measurement of mass removed, scaled up by a heuristic. In 2023 a photogrammetric study finally produced a modern number: [granite removal with a dolerite pounder proceeds at roughly 216 cubic centimetres per hour at 85 strikes a minute]{claim=GEO-C001}, a rate the authors conclude speaks against pounders as the sole method of quarrying. That is one study, one team, one granite and one tool configuration, and skilled crews with maintained tools may do better. It is also the strongest mainstream-legible anomaly in the case. Beside it stand the quarry's stranger features — [vertical shafts some sixteen feet deep, said to be too narrow for a worker to swing a pounder at the bottom]{claim=GEO-C006} — which no one without a stake in the answer has measured.

Be precise about what the rate is evidence *for*. It stresses the pounding-only orthodoxy. It says nothing about casting. A confirmed 216 cubic centimetres an hour is fully compatible with fire-setting, with chisels, or simply with more people and more years than Engelbach allowed.

## The crux

The dispute is narrower than either camp usually admits, and it lives in a question of method.

The strongest conventional evidence class is provenance matching: fingerprinting monument stone by its trace elements and matching it to a quarry, as at Stonehenge. The proponents' most consequential reply is that [the methods used cannot, by design, tell carved quarry stone from stone cast using aggregate gathered at that same quarry]{claim=GEO-C030}. Portable X-ray fluorescence and mass spectrometry cannot see hydrogen, carbon or oxygen — the very elements a water-set binder is made of — and, in Fóti's words, a device with no artificial-stone calibration "will confidently report that it's a natural stone." Crushed West Woods sarsen, carried "in buckets" and cast at Stonehenge, would carry West Woods' metallic fingerprint.

The narrow point is correct. XRF and ICP-MS are indeed blind to those elements, and a quarry match, on its own, cannot exclude casting from that quarry's rubble. But the reply proves less than its proponents want. Fóti's own methods table lists NMR as unable to see carbon, oxygen or silicon, when silicon NMR is a standard technique — and is precisely what the pro-casting Bent Pyramid study used. He himself exempts "petrography, microscopy, acid testing, titration, and so on" from the critique. And petrography is exactly what has been done on Giza stone. Jana's positive control is the decisive demonstration: binder-aware microscopy *does* see a binder when one is there. The provenance-blindness argument therefore qualifies the Stonehenge result, which was never designed to detect casting, and does not touch the direct examinations of pyramid casing stones, which were. The claim is graded mixed for that reason: true as physics, overreaching as an argument.

## The strongest case for casting

An assessment that rejected the hypothesis outright would have to answer this. Peer-reviewed electron microscopy and NMR have reported binder-like phases in monument stone on two continents, and no anti-casting study has yet applied those particular techniques under a blinded, provenance-secure design. Of the four negative studies, two predate the 2006 microscopy and cannot address it; one analysed a sample whose identity is disputed; and the one with a positive control tested a recipe the pro-casting laboratories have since abandoned, while the calcium-silicate binder they now propose has drawn no published rebuttal in more than a decade. Jana himself concedes that a binder at around five per cent by weight might not register in bulk chemistry. The alkaline salt the natron chemistry needs sat in Egypt in industrial quantities. And the only modern measurement of the orthodox quarrying method returned a rate its own authors call insufficient. None of that makes the hypothesis true. It is what keeps it from being closed.

## What would change our mind

The headline claim — [that at least one major megalithic monument, somewhere, contains man-made cast stone]{claim=GEO-C022} — is graded *unresolved*. That is not a shrug but a finding: the one study that would decide it has not been run on any monument. Specifically:

- **Toward casting.** An independent laboratory reproducing the Pumapunku organic and microstructural findings on samples of secure provenance, against natural Khapia andesite controls. A calcium-silicate gel binder found in provenance-secure Giza casing stone by a group outside the Drexel and Geopolymer Institute circles. A blinded paleomagnetic survey finding pyramid blocks whose magnetic remanence aligns with the present field — the signature of stone that set where it stands.
- **Toward carving.** Independent microscopy of Pumapunku andesite finding ordinary volcanic rock. A binder-aware study of secure Giza samples designed to detect a calcium-silicate gel and finding none. Documentation of carved andesite blocks in transit from Cerro Khapia. Halite found effloresced on unworked Giza bedrock, which would remove the salt story's discriminating power entirely.
- **Neither, but clarifying.** A replicated pounding rate several times the 2023 figure would dissolve the Aswan anomaly without bearing on casting at all; a primary Arabic source for the al-Ma'mun salt would make the medieval anchor real without making it diagnostic.

## What would settle it

The case ends in an agenda rather than a verdict. Eleven project designs are attached to the claims they would move, in rough order of how much each decides:

- A blinded paleomagnetic survey of pyramid core blocks against a natural-limestone baseline — the first in-situ physical test of the Great Pyramid claim that does not depend on contested samples.
- A desk check of the Iwawe deposit and the abandoned andesite blocks against the excavators' own descriptions, which moves the Andean claim in either direction for the price of reading.
- A methods audit of published quarry attributions asking, study by study, what each could and could not have detected.
- Sampling unworked Giza and Mokattam limestone for native halite.
- Tracing the al-Ma'mun salt report to its medieval sources.
- Field trials of ultraviolet fluorescence as a cheap screen for alkali-activated material, against known-cast and known-natural panels.
- An audit of restoration histories at Giza, Tiwanaku, Cusco and Easter Island, so that no modern consolidant is mistaken for ancient chemistry.
- Replicating and extending the pounding-rate measurement.
- A criteria-first worldwide catalogue of claimed casting signatures — including where they should appear and do not.
- A joint re-examination of the Rekhmire mural with its inscriptions.
- A controlled long-cycle fire-pit experiment.

The scoop marks at Aswan have waited a long time for someone to measure them properly. Several of the tests above cost little more than a library card. What the record lacks is not ingenuity but the study that nobody has yet paid for.

assessment.synthesis: The featured thesis (GEO-C022) is existential — one cast monument anywhere suffices — so the case verdict is not an average across branches. The Egyptian branch is the only one tested with binder-aware methods on monument stone, and the record there is a genuine collision rather than weak one-sided support: peer-reviewed microscopy and NMR for (GEO-E012, GEO-E017) against field petrography across many blocks (GEO-E018), the Lauer-sample examination (GEO-E019), the positive-control study (GEO-E020) and an independent museum fragment (GEO-E021). The balance leans against, because every binder-aware examination by a group outside the pro-casting circle concludes natural rock and GEO-E020 shows that an alkali binder would be visible if present; but the negatives hinge on physical-object disputes (Lauer sample identity, Drexel sample origin) and GEO-E020 tests a recipe the affirmative side has since replaced with a calcium-silicate gel that has drawn no published rebuttal. Hence GEO-C020 is mixed, not weakly supported and not contradicted. The Andean branch (GEO-E006, GEO-E007) is one team, one sample set, contested custody, never independently rerun; the sole counterweight, GEO-E008, is a 1971 provenance study of sandstones set against microscopy of andesite, so the halves of GEO-C021 receive evidence in opposite directions on different lithologies and neither is tested by anyone else. The proponents' methods critique (GEO-C030, GEO-E024) is correct in its narrow form — XRF and ICP-MS cannot see H, C or O, so a quarry match such as GEO-E009 cannot by itself exclude casting from quarry aggregate — but overreaches: its own table misstates NMR, and GEO-E020 demonstrates that binder-aware petrography detects binders. The Aswan material (GEO-E001, GEO-E003, GEO-E005) bears on the completeness of the pounding-only orthodoxy, not on casting. The salt anchors (GEO-E004, GEO-E026) are untraced and uncontrolled, with the wrong comparator. The case is unresolved rather than mixed because the collision exists only in Egypt and turns there on disputes about which object was analysed and which recipe was tested, while the decisive design — a blinded, provenance-secure, binder-aware comparison scored against prespecified criteria — has not been run on any monument. The single record whose removal would most change the verdict is GEO-E020: it is the only positive-control study, it anchors the Egyptian negative and it is the principal answer to GEO-C030; without it GEO-C020 would move toward weakly_supported and GEO-C030 toward provisionally_supported, and the case toward mixed.
assessment.steelman: Peer-reviewed electron microscopy (GEO-E012) and multinuclear NMR (GEO-E017) have reported binder-like phases in monument stone on two continents (with GEO-E006/E007), and no anti-casting study has applied those same techniques under a blinded, provenance-secure design. Of the four negative records, GEO-E018 and GEO-E019 predate the 2006 microscopy and cannot address its specific microconstituents; GEO-E019 and GEO-E020 analysed a piece whose identity as the Lauer sample is disputed; and GEO-E020, the only study with a positive control, tested the alkali-aluminosilicate recipe rather than the calcium-silicate gel now proposed, which has stood without published rebuttal since 2011 while GEO-E022 shows that gel forms at room temperature from lime and diatomaceous earth. Jana concedes a binder near 5 wt% might not register in bulk chemistry. GEO-E021 is one museum fragment whose authors themselves flag sampling adequacy. Meanwhile the natron the chemistry needs is documented at industrial scale (GEO-E010), and the only modern measurement of the orthodox quarrying method (GEO-E001) returns a rate its own authors call insufficient for pounders alone. Taken together: the affirmative evidence has not been refuted on its own terms, only on superseded ones.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: At least one major megalithic monument contains man-made cast stone: blocks produced on site by binding processed mineral inputs (alkali geopolymer, natron-derived waterglass, lime–silica gel, or related chemistry) rather than by carving natural rock alone. The strongest specific versions name Great Pyramid casing and backing blocks and the andesite and sandstone of Pumapunku.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether anomalies exist — a measured pounding rate, proponent SEM and NMR findings, a salt report — but over three narrower things: whether the physical samples analysed on each side are what they are said to be (the Lauer sample, the Drexel samples, the Pumapunku set); whether the negative petrography, which decisively tested an alkali binder with a positive control, also rules out the calcium-silicate binder the affirmative side now proposes; and whether quarry-matching geochemistry, which is blind to hydrogen, carbon and oxygen, constrains casting at all — a point that is true of provenance methods and false of the binder-aware microscopy that has actually been applied to Giza stone.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: For the Great Pyramid: a blinded comparison of provenance-secure casing and backing samples against geologically matched Mokattam and Tura limestone, scored against prespecified signatures for both an alkali-aluminosilicate and a calcium-silicate gel binder, ideally paired with a paleomagnetic survey of core blocks against a natural-remanence baseline. For Pumapunku: independent SEM and petrographic re-analysis of secure andesite samples against natural Khapia andesite controls, plus a reading of the Iwawe excavation record for what the claimed aggregate deposit actually is. Either result at either site would be decisive for that monument; a negative at both would leave the existential thesis without any tested positive.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Quarrying, carving and transport with well-attested means: dolerite pounders and copper tools, fire-setting, ramps, sledges, levers and large organised labour forces. The account is supported by unfinished monuments abandoned mid-extraction at quarries, tool marks and tools at extraction sites, worker settlements, experimental carving demonstrations, sedimentary and fossil features observed in situ in pyramid blocks, binder-aware petrography of pyramid casing stones finding natural limestone, and geochemical provenance matching monument stone to specific quarries. Its gaps are quantitative — extraction rates, labour, timelines, specific quarry features — not existential; it requires no unattested technology.

components.label: Existential thesis (cast stone in at least one monument)
components.note: No monument has received the decisive blinded, provenance-secure, binder-aware test; the one tested branch turns on sample-identity disputes and a superseded recipe.

components.label: Great Pyramid casting (Egyptian branch)
components.note: Peer-reviewed SEM/TEM and NMR positives against four petrographic negatives including one with a positive control; balance leans against for the alkali recipe, calcium-silicate binder untested.

components.label: Pumapunku casting (Andean branch)
components.note: Proponent-only SEM/petrography on andesite; 1971 provenance of sandstones to natural quarries; the two lines address different lithologies and neither is independently replicated.

components.label: Feasibility of artificial limestone
components.note: Demonstration blocks are self-reported; lime–silica gel chemistry is established; feasibility is not occurrence.

components.label: Ingredient availability (natron)
components.note: Industrial-scale Egyptian natron and its 7th–9th-century decline are mainstream findings about glass; they say nothing about stone.

components.label: Methods critique of quarry-matching
components.note: H/C/O blindness of XRF and ICP-MS is real; the extension to all analytical methods is wrong (NMR misstated) and is answered by binder-aware petrography with a positive control.

components.label: Aswan quarrying-rate anomaly
components.note: One peer-reviewed measurement stresses the pounding-only account; compatible with fire-setting, chisels or more labour; no bearing on casting.

components.label: Historical anchors (salt report, Rekhmire mural, fire-pit origin)
components.note: Untraced, uncontrolled or unattributed proponent reports; none tested.

researchPriority.reason: Several cheap, decisive tests exist — reading the Iwawe excavation record, tracing the al-Ma'mun report, sampling unworked Giza bedrock for halite — and a provenance-secure binder-aware comparison would settle specific monuments in either direction. Against that, the prior for the thesis is low, the mainstream account is not in crisis, and much of the agenda is confound-killing rather than discovery; the value is in closing a forty-five-year dispute cheaply, not in a likely overturning.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Existential claim decided by its strongest instance. Egypt: GEO-E012 and GEO-E017 (moderate, for) against GEO-E018, GEO-E019, GEO-E020 (strong) and GEO-E021 (moderate, against); the negatives dominate for the alkali recipe but rest on disputed sample identities and leave the calcium-silicate proposal untested. Andes: GEO-E006/E007 (one team, contested custody) with only the oblique GEO-E008 against. Stonehenge: GEO-E009 fits natural sourcing but is not cast-aware. No monument has had the decisive test, so the claim is neither supported nor refuted on the record.

treatment.plainLanguage: Somewhere in the world, at least one great monument includes stone that was made like concrete rather than cut from bedrock.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the thesis itself; every other claim is evidence for or against it, and a single confirmed instance would carry it.
treatment.strongestObjection: Every binder-aware examination of monument stone by a group outside the pro-casting circle has concluded natural rock, and the one study with a positive control showed that a casting signature would be plainly visible if present.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent laboratory reproduction of the Pumapunku findings on provenance-secure samples against natural Khapia andesite controls.
A calcium-silicate gel binder found in provenance-secure Great Pyramid casing stone by a group independent of the Drexel and Geopolymer Institute teams.
A blinded, binder-aware study of secure Giza samples targeting both proposed binders and finding neither, together with independent microscopy of Pumapunku andesite finding ordinary volcanic rock.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E012 (SEM/TEM microconstituents, non-proponent but sample origin contested, authors concede nature could produce all features) and GEO-E017 (NMR read as calcium-silicate gel, one stone, Barsoum co-author) support; GEO-E018 (sedimentary and fossil features in situ across many blocks, tool marks, no zeolite), GEO-E019 (Lauer sample natural Mokattam limestone), GEO-E020 (positive control shows alkali binder detectable, none in casing stones, Barsoum's spheres are natural opal-CT) and GEO-E021 (independent BM fragment natural by five techniques) undermine. Balance leans against for the tested alkali recipe, but the Lauer-sample identity and Drexel-sample provenance are genuine physical disputes and GEO-E020 does not test the C–S–H binder. GEO-E022 shows only feasibility; GEO-E023 fixes scope to casings, tops and backing blocks.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some of the Great Pyramid's blocks — especially the smooth outer casing — were poured and set, not quarried and cut.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If true for even the casing stones, the existential thesis is established; if the casing stones are natural, the best-tested branch of the hypothesis falls.
treatment.strongestObjection: Pyramid blocks show bedding, burrows, sharp fossil cross-sections and tectonic fractures confined within blocks, and side-by-side petrography with a genuine geopolymer control finds none of the binder enrichment the control plainly shows.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A blinded examination of provenance-secure casing and backing samples designed to detect a calcium-silicate gel: finding it would move the claim toward supported, finding none would move it toward contradicted.
Resolution of the Lauer-sample identity dispute, which would either restore or remove the force of GEO-E019 and GEO-E020's Lauer findings.
A blinded paleomagnetic survey of core blocks against a natural-limestone remanence baseline (GEO-R011).

claimAssessments.reasoning: The andesite half is supported by GEO-E006 and GEO-E007 (peer-reviewed venues, but one team, one sample set, contested custody, no independent replication, criteria not blind-tested). The sandstone half is undermined by GEO-E008 (1971 provenance to natural quarries, pre-modern methods). The two lithologies receive evidence in opposite directions and never on the same material; neither has been tested by anyone outside the proponents or after 1971.

treatment.plainLanguage: The grey H-blocks and red sandstone slabs at Pumapunku were cast from a mineral paste rather than carved.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A confirmed cast andesite block at Pumapunku would establish the existential thesis on its own; a natural finding would remove the only positive laboratory evidence outside Egypt.
treatment.strongestObjection: The only positives come from the hypothesis's own proponents on samples of contested custody, volcanic rock naturally hosts organic and glassy phases, and the sandstones have been attributed to natural quarries.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent SEM and petrographic re-analysis of provenance-secure andesite against natural Khapia andesite controls.

The Iwawe Stratum V deposit and the abandoned andesite blocks checked against the excavators' descriptions (GEO-R009): documented carved ashlars in transit would undermine wholesale casting, a natural sand store would give the proponent model a non-trivial prediction.
Modern provenance re-analysis of the sandstones and a restoration-history audit (GEO-R005) excluding modern consolidants as the source of the organics.

claimAssessments.reasoning: As worded this is a descriptive claim about published analyses, and GEO-E006 and GEO-E007 establish that the analyses exist in peer-reviewed venues and report organic matter and microstructural features interpreted as artificial. What is not established is the substantive content — that the features are inconsistent with natural andesite — because the two records are one team and one sample set, the discriminating criteria were not blind-tested, and volcanic rocks can host organic and glassy phases. Nothing in the ledger directly undermines the claim; the incumbent 'mixed' had no undermining record behind it.

treatment.plainLanguage: Two published studies looked at Pumapunku stone under electron microscopes and found things — including organic material — that the authors say volcanic rock should not contain.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Credible as a report of what was published; weak as evidence for casting until reproduced independently, because the criteria for 'unnatural' were set by the proponents and never tested against known natural andesite. If independently confirmed, this would become the most diagnostic observation in the case.
treatment.strongestObjection: Same team, same sample set, contested chain of custody, and no natural-andesite control examined blind; organic and glassy phases occur in natural volcanic rock.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent replication of the SEM and petrographic findings on secure samples with natural controls.
A restoration-history audit showing modern consolidants or mortar at the sampled locations, which would supply a mundane source for the organics.
Blind testing of the proponents' discriminating criteria against natural Khapia andesite.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E024 makes the narrow point correctly: PXRF and ICP-MS cannot detect hydrogen, carbon or oxygen, so a quarry match alone cannot exclude casting from that quarry's aggregate, and this legitimately qualifies GEO-E009. But the same record documents that Fóti's methods table misstates NMR (²⁹Si NMR is standard and is what GEO-E017 used), and GEO-E020 undermines the extension by showing that binder-aware petrography with a positive control detects binders when present. GEO-E009 undermines only insofar as it shows provenance evidence fitting conventional sourcing.

treatment.plainLanguage: The chemical fingerprinting used to trace stones to quarries cannot see the ingredients of a cement, so 'we found the quarry' does not by itself rule out stones cast from that quarry's rubble.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decides how much the strongest conventional evidence class constrains the hypothesis, not whether casting happened; even if fully granted it removes an objection rather than adding support.
treatment.strongestObjection: The critique exempts petrography and microscopy by its author's own admission, and petrography with a positive control has been applied to Giza casing stone and found natural limestone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A methods audit (GEO-R003) showing that immobile-element ratios shift detectably with binder additives, which would weaken the claim.
A demonstration that a block cast from crushed West Woods sarsen passes the Nash et al. 2020 protocol unchanged, which would strengthen the narrow claim.
Binder-aware re-examination of provenance-matched stones at Stonehenge or Tiwanaku.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E013 reports multi-ton demonstration blocks but is self-reported by the proponent organisation with no independent analysis; GEO-E022 establishes that lime and diatomaceous earth form a calcium-silicate gel binder at room temperature; GEO-E012 contributes only indirectly. The verdict also leans on the general prior that geopolymer and lime-silica chemistry is established materials science; the ledger lacks an independent analysis of any demonstration block.

treatment.plainLanguage: It is possible, using materials and heat available to ancient builders, to make a hard block that looks like natural limestone.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Necessary for the thesis but nowhere near sufficient: modern feasibility says nothing about ancient practice, and the claim is compatible with every monument being carved.
treatment.strongestObjection: No demonstration block has been independently analysed, and feasibility at bench or single-block scale is not feasibility at the scale of millions of blocks.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent petrographic analysis of a Geopolymer Institute demonstration block confirming or refuting its stated composition and strength.
A scale-up experiment producing casing-quality blocks with documented ancient-feasible inputs and labour.
Failure of independent attempts to reproduce the demonstration blocks with the stated recipes.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E010 (strong, mainstream peer-reviewed) identifies Wadi el Natrun and al-Barnuj as the ancient natron sources for the vitreous-materials industry with a documented 7th–9th-century decline; GEO-E011 supplies the compositional typology behind such timelines. The paper concerns glass and faience and makes no claim about stone.

treatment.plainLanguage: Ancient Egypt had large natural deposits of natron, used them for centuries, and lost the supply in the early medieval period.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Establishes that a key ingredient was available; availability of an ingredient is not evidence of its use for stone-making, and the documented uses are glass, faience and mummification.
treatment.strongestObjection: No Egyptian text or archaeological context connects natron to stone production; the supply discontinuity has a conventional explanation in the glass industry's shift to plant ash.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Evidence that Old Kingdom exploitation of the natron sources was small-scale or late, which would weaken the availability argument for the pyramid age.
Glass-composition timelines (via the GEO-E011 typology) showing natron supply anomalies coincident with major construction periods, which would strengthen the story.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The only record is GEO-E016, a weak proponent citation of early glassmaking whose dating and temperature basis are unverified. The verdict leans on the background prior that ~850 °C is modest for ancient pyrotechnology; the ledger itself provides little.

treatment.plainLanguage: Ancient furnaces could reach the heat needed to make waterglass from natron and sand.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A necessary condition that almost everyone grants; crucible-scale heat is not industrial-scale processing, and the claim says nothing about whether stone was made.
treatment.strongestObjection: Reaching 850 °C in a crucible is not the same as sustaining it across the volumes casting-scale production would require, and the Badari precedent is unverified.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent verification of the Badari glass dating and firing temperatures.
Archaeological evidence of large-scale furnaces or ash deposits at claimed production sites — or documented absence where the hypothesis predicts them.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E015 is a single unattributed anecdote recounted by a proponent and flagged as under-sourced; no controlled replication exists. There is no record against it either.

treatment.plainLanguage: A fire pit used for years might accidentally turn its ash into rock, which is how people could first have discovered stone-making.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: An origin story, not evidence of ancient practice; confirming it would make the hypothesis more intuitive without making it more probable, and failing it would remove a narrative rather than a pillar.
treatment.strongestObjection: An unattributed anecdote with no measurement, and ash-carbonation producing weakly cemented crust is far from monument-grade stone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A controlled multi-month fire-pit experiment (GEO-R007) producing — or failing to produce — structurally stone-like material.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E001 is a peer-reviewed photogrammetric measurement giving 216 cm³/h at 85 strikes/min with the authors' own conclusion against pounders alone; GEO-E002 provides context that the orthodox rate rests on Engelbach's thin 1922 basis, though that characterisation is Fóti's and unverified against the monograph. Single study, single team, single configuration.

treatment.plainLanguage: When someone finally measured how fast a dolerite pounder removes granite, the answer was slow — about a coffee-mug of rock per hour.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Stresses the pounding-only account of Aswan quarrying; says nothing about casting, since a slow rate is fully compatible with fire-setting, chisels, or more workers and years.
treatment.strongestObjection: One experimental protocol; skilled ancient crews with maintained tools and fire-setting may far outperform a modern trial.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent replication (GEO-R002) with sensitivity to technique, tool mass and granite type: a rate several times higher would dissolve the anomaly.
Verification of Engelbach's actual method against the 1922 and 1923 texts.
Independent documentation of fire-setting debris at the Unfinished Obelisk quarry.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E003 is an anecdote with no count of attempts, no measure of cumulative effort and no survey of the test block; GEO-E002 is context only. Nothing in the ledger tests it in either direction.

treatment.plainLanguage: Tourists have been hitting a test block at Aswan with ancient pounders for decades and none has made a scoop mark.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even if true it shows only that casual strikes do not produce scoops; a scoop represents hours of sustained work, so the observation bears weakly on the orthodoxy and not at all on casting.
treatment.strongestObjection: Uncounted, unmeasured casual attempts by untrained visitors are not a test of a quarrying method.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A wear survey of the test block quantifying cumulative removal.
A controlled attempt by trained workers to produce a scoop mark with dolerite pounders.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E005 is a proponent description; shaft dimensions have not been independently surveyed and the biomechanical claim is untested.

treatment.plainLanguage: There are deep, narrow shafts beside the unfinished obelisk that a worker could not have pounded out from inside.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If confirmed it points to some other extraction technique at the shaft bottoms, which need not be casting-related; the proponents' alternative reading of the shafts as processing vessels is a separate, untested claim.
treatment.strongestObjection: No measurement exists; shafts may have been cut with other tools, from above, or by fire-setting, and their function is unknown.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A published survey of shaft dimensions with a biomechanical assessment of feasible strike postures.
Documentation of tool marks or debris at the shaft bottoms.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E004 is a secondary report on a proponent website, untraced to any primary Arabic source within the case, and the salt has mundane candidate origins. No record confirms or refutes the medieval account.

treatment.plainLanguage: A ninth-century story says that when the caliph's men broke into the Great Pyramid they found the walls crusted with salt.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even a genuine medieval report of salt would not discriminate cast from natural stone, since limestone in enclosed chambers effloresces salts for ordinary reasons; the report is an anchor for the natron narrative, not a test of it.
treatment.strongestObjection: The report has no located primary source, and natural efflorescence, mortar and groundwater are ordinary explanations for salt on limestone chamber walls.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Tracing the account to a medieval author (GEO-R001): a credible source makes the anchor real; absence or embellishment removes it.
Finding halite native to unworked Giza and Mokattam limestone (GEO-R010), which would remove any discriminating power the salt might have.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E026 is an uncontrolled taste test with no quantities, no instrument and no named comparator, and its offered comparator (European cathedrals) is the wrong lithology; the ledger has no measurement of salt on pyramid stone and no comparison with unworked Giza or Mokattam bedrock. The editor's own inference treats the record as effectively weightless.

treatment.plainLanguage: Pyramid stones taste salty and, the proponents say, natural limestone buildings do not.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Without the right comparator the observation cannot distinguish anything; if unworked Giza limestone also effloresces halite, the salt story collapses, and if it does not, the salt becomes an anomaly worth bulk-chlorine testing but still not proof of casting.
treatment.strongestObjection: A tongue is not an instrument, a cathedral is not a control, and salt efflorescence on limestone in enclosed spaces is a familiar conservation phenomenon.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: XRD analysis of efflorescence from protected unworked Giza and Mokattam bedrock and quarry faces alongside a Queen's Chamber reference (GEO-R010).
Bulk rather than surface chlorine measurements on provenance-secure pyramid stone against natural comparators.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E014 is a proponent's interpretive argument; conventional Egyptology reads the scene as metal casting and has not engaged the reinterpretation, and the scene's inscriptions have not been brought to bear in the ledger.

treatment.plainLanguage: A tomb painting usually read as bronze-founders casting a door might instead show workers processing minerals.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A reinterpretation of an image cannot establish a technology; at most it would supply a period depiction consistent with casting, and the conventional reading has textual support the case has not yet weighed.
treatment.strongestObjection: The scene is captioned and contextualised within a corpus of metalworking depictions, and no Egyptologist has found the bronze reading wanting.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A joint Egyptological and history-of-technology re-examination (GEO-R008) weighing the inscriptions and apparatus against each reading.
Archaeological residues at the depicted scale matching one process and not the other.
